name: Tamanu oil

lead: Tamanu oil is a viscous green-yellow oil from the nuts of a coastal tropical tree, used in Polynesia, India and Southeast Asia for wounds, burns and skin conditions. In natural skincare it is used to fade scars and acne marks and calm breakouts.
In cell studies a Polynesian tamanu oil emulsion raised skin-cell proliferation and collagen production, and the oil shows antioxidant activity. Human trials for scars or acne were not found.

paras: People apply it as a few drops directly on marks or scars, or mix it into creams and carrier oils, usually over weeks to months. Its strong scent and thick texture mean it is often blended.
It is reported as low in toxicity at low concentrations; allergy data are limited. As a nut-derived oil it may matter to people with nut allergy.

angle.text: Tamanu oil is used to fade scars and acne marks and calm breakouts, building on traditional Pacific use for wounds and burns. Lab studies on skin cells show raised proliferation and collagen production; human trials were not found.

lead: Tamanu oil is a viscous green-yellow oil pressed from the nuts of Calophyllum inophyllum, a tropical tree of the Indo-Pacific. It has been used in traditional medicine in Polynesia, India and Southeast Asia for wounds, burns and skin conditions.[1][2]

In skincare it is promoted for scars and acne. Laboratory work reports that a Polynesian tamanu oil emulsion stimulated proliferation and collagen production in cultured human skin cells,[3] but the sources reviewed describe no completed clinical trial for scars or acne.

paras: The oil is bluish-yellow to dark green and viscous, with a resin fraction of 10 to 30 percent; main fatty acids are oleic, linoleic, stearic and palmitic, and it contains compounds such as calophyllolide and 4-phenylcoumarins.[1] Composition varies by geographic origin across the South Pacific.[4]
Most commercial use is in skin care.[1] Grokipedia lists its INCI name and a comedogenic rating of 2 attributed to a safety source.[2]

In vitro, a Polynesian tamanu oil emulsion promoted keratinocyte and fibroblast proliferation and glycosaminoglycan and collagen production.[3] A 2021 review discusses its potential for atopic dermatitis, based largely on preclinical work.[5] Formulation papers use tamanu oil as a delivery component.[6]
Grokipedia reports low toxicity and no irritation at low concentrations; Wikipedia does not discuss allergy.[1][2]
